result.label: Own-price elasticity, 330ml can
result.rationale: Smallest, most impulse-driven format; set near the elastic end of the brief's -0.8 to -2.5 CPG range.
result.reference: Context only, not a fitted value. A 2024 meta-analysis of U.S. food demand elasticities (Jeon, Hoang, Thompson and Abler) finds household scanner data tends to give more elastic own-price estimates (https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/a-meta-analysis-of-us-food-demand-elasticities-to-detect-the-impa/). It does not cover soft drinks specifically, so the values here are illustrative. A Marketing Science Institute working paper (Bray, Sanders and Stamatopoulos) finds observational scanner price variation does not reproduce experimental elasticities (https://www.msi.org/working-paper/observational-price-variation-in-scanner-data-cannot-reproduce-experimental-price-elasticities/), so the value carries a range that drives the sensitivity bands.

caveats: All modeled options share the same underlying market and elasticity assumptions, so if those are wrong the relative profit and volume impacts could differ in reality.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: At the current 330 ml can price, the focal brand delivers weekly gross profit of ₹2,27,764 with can volume of 3,786 units and serves as the baseline for comparison.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: Under a 3% price increase on the 330 ml can, weekly gross profit for the focal brand falls to ₹2,26,442 and can volume drops to 3,537 units, a decline of more than 5% versus baseline, mainly driven by the price rise and associated volume loss partially offset by better cost of goods and small positive cross-pack effects.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: At a near-upper observed price for the 330 ml can, focal weekly gross profit declines further to ₹2,24,296 and can volume to 3,171 units, with the higher price unable to offset the larger volume loss despite some improvement in cost of goods and modest cross-pack gains.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: At the stretch price for the 330 ml can, focal weekly gross profit is lowest at ₹2,23,461 and can volume falls to 3,040 units, as the aggressive price cut to demand sharply reduces volume and more than offsets gains from higher unit price, improved cost of goods and cross-pack shifts.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: The Gabor-Granger research identified ₹36 and ₹40 as candidate 330 ml can prices from synthetic consumer responses, with ₹40 aligning with the current modeled shelf price that maximizes weekly gross profit among the tested scenarios.

claims.label: Modeled
claims.text: Under the downside input-cost stress with unchanged shelf prices, focal weekly gross profit drops to ₹2,16,721 due solely to higher cost of goods, without any modeled change in volumes or prices.

claims.label: Observed
claims.text: The candidate Gabor-Granger revenue-index maximum price scenario for the 330 ml can, which requested a material price cut, could not be evaluated because Aurora-can_330ml: price_index 0.9 outside observed 1st-99th percentile [0.9424, 1.1082].

recommendations: Hold the 330 ml can at the current price, as this maintains the highest weekly gross profit of ₹2,27,764 with no volume loss versus baseline and already sits at the modeled consumer upper-acceptance price.

Do not implement the 3% price increase on the 330 ml can, because weekly gross profit falls to ₹2,26,442 and can volume drops by more than 5% versus baseline, driven mainly by the price rise and volume loss.

Do not implement the near-upper observed price increase on the 330 ml can, as weekly gross profit falls further to ₹2,24,296 and can volume drops well beyond 5% versus baseline, with the higher price not offsetting the sharper volume decline.
Do not implement the stretch price increase on the 330 ml can, since weekly gross profit is lowest at ₹2,23,461 and the largest volume loss comes from the aggressive price move.
refusals: Aurora-can_330ml: price_index 0.9 outside observed 1st-99th percentile [0.9424, 1.1082] – this option cannot be evaluated and should not be used for a pricing decision.
answer.summary: Keep the 330 ml can at its current price; all modeled price increases reduce weekly gross profit and push volume losses beyond the 5% limit versus baseline.
